I accepted AD3 for what it was meant to show. The native C# route now knows which files belong to which project in all three test repositories, which was AD3's target.

AD3 does not show that native C# matches legacy. Of 50 sampled requests, native matched legacy on 8, improved on none, and lost targets on 23. Every native answer was marked incomplete. The #9947 slowdown is confirmed and explained. When reuse is refused, master recomputes every result it has just computed, which costs about 45 seconds per Bat run. A small fix that keeps the first results changes no answer and can land now, with no cache token.

The deeper reason Bat reuses nothing is that one test file anywhere in the repository has a parse error. That marks every stored result as depending on how the run went, rather than on the code, so none can be reused. I approved the lane's next design, which labels each gap by its actual cause, under strict rules. A gap counts as code-determined only if the stored result records the file it came from, so fixing that file invalidates the result. Any cause not on an explicit list stays run-dependent.

Mapping the #9947 work turned up a possible soundness bug already on master. Some stored taint results built from a cached lookup may not record what that lookup read. If so, an edit that changes those inputs would not invalidate the stored result, and a stale "complete" answer could be reused. 07d292ca is building a test case to check. If the bug is real, the fix lands first, as its own change with a cache token, so that results already stored under the old code are invalidated too.

The #9947 speed fix is now narrower and safe. It keeps the first computed results only when reuse was refused because of the answers themselves. If the refusal came from the run, such as a failed read or a change to the workspace during the solve, it recomputes as before. The Bat savings are unchanged.

**Master has a serious performance regression.** With the Rust standard-library pack enabled, registering policies takes over 1,500 seconds even on a two-file test repository. Without that pack it takes 57 seconds, and an earlier master finished the same check. c2a66e1c is bisecting it, and the suspects include two close-match commits, #10134 and #10144. I will see the fix before it touches anything that affects caching.

I also ruled on a close-match bug. A pack built for one version of a dependency could also be activated for other versions of that dependency in the same graph. The matcher gets fixed first. At run time, a version outside the pack's range is reported as missing evidence. Filtering per version is allowed only if lookups are scoped by package; otherwise the whole pack is refused.

Rust looks up packs by crate name only, so the close-match lane is refusing the whole pack when a resolved dependency version falls outside its range. The refused version appears in the external inventory output under the existing `missing_evidence` status, with a new reason, so clients see no new status value. It needs no cache version, because the inventory is recomputed for each request. Nothing here needs your decision.

Two rulings from this round matter beyond the lane involved.

- **The #10301 fix may cost precision broadly.** The first version of the fix is sound: Rust code that reads a name it cannot resolve in its own file gets refused. But if that refusal shows up as an ordinary gap, then every Rust function that reads an imported constant or function would turn its taint and policy answers partial, not only the protocol publication the lane described. I required either that the refusal stay inside the coverage check, or a count of how many answers become partial before it lands.
- **Refused close-match versions use an existing status.** A dependency version refused by its close-match pack shows as `incompatible`, the existing status for a pack whose version requirement does not match, with the new reason text. So client output gains no new status value. My first ruling assumed an external `missing_evidence` status that does not exist.

Waiting on: the bisection of the standard-library regression and the end of the #9687 r10 run.

I accepted #9559's design that ties its JDK checks to the files' actual bytes. It also closes an old gap where a cached JDK pack could be reused based only on file metadata. One cost to know about: on Windows, every JVM request will re-hash the JDK's module files, about 1.6 seconds each time, until a follow-up adds the Windows file identity it needs. I asked for that follow-up and a Windows measurement before the later 3d step.

Maven projects and projects with explicit jar paths are not affected. The lane will file a separate issue for Gradle.

I accepted #9559's narrower handling of cancellation. When a Java read is cancelled, the lane records that on the query, using a flag that already exists and that tools already report, instead of adding an error return through 14 layers of wrappers. The main condition: a result from a cancelled read must never be cached, so the next request gets a full answer. Nothing here needs your decision.

For #10301, I accepted a narrow rule for recognizing a call to a function declared in the same module, with one Rust-specific catch. Code can declare a function and a static under the same name, each enabled by a different build configuration. The syntax tree shows both at once, so a rule that reads only the syntax tree could take the function where the active build actually reads the static. Declarations gated on a build configuration, names also brought in by an import, and names declared more than once therefore do not count as proof. Nothing here needs your decision.
